scenario: AITA for "taking" a disabled students seat? | I'm currently taking a class at my local college. The class is MWF but last Monday was a holiday so the first day of class was last Wednesday. I attended the first day of class but it was packed so I had to stand in the back. Then I missed the Friday lecture as well as the Monday lecture. Today, Wednesday, was my 1st day back. I knew the class was packed so I came 10 min early to get a seat in the front row. I prefer to sit in the front row because I have anxiety. By sitting in the front I'm able to ask questions/answer questions without being forced to shout it across the room. I'm perfectly capable of doing well in a course if I'm forced to sit in the back...this is just a strong preference. All seats are first come, first served. There are 2 seats in each class called "priority seats" specifically designated for the disabled that are only open to abled students when they're unoccupied. You have to notify the school, then the professor makes sure that seat is available to you every lecture. For the abled seats, after a few weeks people always tend to sit in the same seats and you get the impression that its your "seat" that you sit in for the rest of the semester even though its technically not. After I sit down I notice 2 girls walk in together talking and laughing. One girl sits in the seat behind me and the other girl stands next to me and says: Girl 1: Hi, sorry, actually you're sitting in my seat. Me: There is no assigned seating. Anyone can sit anywhere. Girl 1: Yeah but I've been sitting in this seat all semester (this is our 3rd lecture out of like 30). There are still open seats in the back that you can move to. Me: Which means there are also open seats in the back that you can sit in too, right? Girl 1: Look...I'm deaf in 1 ear. I need a seat in the front row. Move please. (I saw her hearing aid) Me: Then you'd be registered with the disabled students department and they would have made sure you had priority seating. This isn't a priority seat. Girl 1: I don't need to register anything with the school and I dont need to explain myself to you. Its my seat...I told you I need it because I'm hard of hearing. Me: Wouldn't those same rules apply to me as well? Not needing to explain myself to you? Girl 2: Stop being an asshole and just fucking move...jesus. Me: I'm done talking. I'm not moving. Girl 1 and Girl 2: \*\*scoffs\*\* Girl 1: \*\*finds another seat\*\* I don't feel like I did anything wrong, but I damn sure spent the rest of class overhearing everyone behind me talking shit about me. It's important to point out that we're always given worksheets that we can work on with the person behind us...so its possible Girl 1 mostly wanted my seat so she could work with Girl 2 on it. Also, I was in the front seat in the far left corner. There are about 10 seats closer to the middle board than the seat I was in.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me start by understanding the situation. The person is a Muslim student who has anxiety and prefers sitting in the front row of their class. They went early to secure a seat because the class is usually packed. They took a seat in the front row, which isn't a priority seat for the disabled. Then, two girls come in, one of whom says she's been sitting there all semester and needs it because she's hard of hearing. The student responds by pointing out that there are other seats available and that the priority seats are for registered disabled students. The girl gets upset and tells the student to move, and her friend tells the student to just move. The student doesn't move and feels like they did nothing wrong, but they overheard others talking negatively about them. So, the question is whether the student's action of not moving from the seat is morally acceptable. First, I need to consider the rules of the class. It says that all seats are first come, first served, except for the priority seats which are reserved for disabled students. The student took a regular seat, not a priority one. The girl claimed she's been sitting there all semester, implying it's her usual spot, but she's not registered as disabled. She mentioned being hard of hearing but didn't go through the proper channels to get a priority seat. The student's reasoning was that since the girl isn't registered, she shouldn't take a priority seat. But the girl argued that she needs the front seat because of her hearing issue. The student pointed out that there are other seats available, so the girl could sit elsewhere. Now, from a moral standpoint, the student was following the rules by taking a first-come seat. They didn't take a priority seat, which is reserved for those who have registered. The girl, on the other hand, was trying to claim a seat without going through the proper process, even though she has a disability. The student was standing their ground based on the established rules. However, the girl had a valid need for a front seat due to her hearing. But since she didn't register, she didn't have the priority. The student was correct in pointing out that there are other seats available, so the girl could have sat elsewhere. The student's refusal to move wasn't about being stubborn but about adhering to the rules. Additionally, the student's anxiety is a factor. They prefer the front row to feel more comfortable and engaged in class. It's a strong preference, not just a want, which makes their desire to keep the seat more understandable. The fact that the student didn't move and that others were talking negatively about them afterward adds some emotional stress, but that doesn't necessarily make the action wrong. The student was within their rights according to the class rules. So, considering all this, the student's action seems morally acceptable because they followed the rules, didn't take a priority seat, and the girl didn't have the right to claim that seat without registration. The student's preference for the front row is valid, especially given their anxiety, and they handled the situation by pointing out the rules rather than giving in without reason.
